passages.t: Jehoiada brings out the king's son
passages.happening:
In the seventh year Jehoiada the priest makes a covenant with the commanders of hundreds (verse 1). They gather the Levites and the family heads from all Judah to Jerusalem, ‘the whole assembly made a covenant with the king in the house of God’ (verse 3), and Jehoiada says, “Behold, the king’s son!” (verse 3), and that he must reign, ‘just as the LORD promised concerning the descendants of David’ (verse 3).

He sets the priests and Levites coming on duty on the Sabbath to guard the doors, the palace and the gate; only those consecrated may enter the house of the LORD (verses 4-7). He gives the commanders the spears and shields of King David that were kept in the temple (verse 9). ‘Then Jehoiada and his sons brought out the king’s son, put the crown on him, presented him with the Testimony, and proclaimed him king’ (verse 11). They anoint him and shout, “Long live the king!” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 22 ended with David's line reduced to one hidden child and Ahab's daughter ruling Judah. This chapter tells how the lamp of David was set back on its stand. Athaliah ruled about six years, around 841 to 835 BC. The priest Jehoiada acts as guardian of both the promise to David and the temple, and the coup is carried out largely by priests and Levites inside the house of God.

Service was organized in divisions that changed over on the Sabbath. Jehoiada kept both the incoming and the outgoing divisions on duty, doubling his men in the temple without raising suspicion. David's own spears and shields, dedicated in the temple, now guard David's heir.

Second Kings 11 tells the same story with different emphases: there the guards include the Carites, probably foreign mercenaries, and the royal guard; here the Levites and family heads lead, and the text insists that only consecrated priests and Levites entered the temple. Many think the Chronicler shaped the account to show the coup done according to the law's rules for the sanctuary; others think he drew on more information about the Levites' part. Both agree on the core events.

The coronation has several parts. The crown marked the office. The Testimony, edut, was probably a written copy of the covenant law or the king's obligations, linked by many with Deuteronomy's command that the king keep a copy of the law. Anointing, mashach, set him apart; from it comes mashiach, Messiah. The shout was the people's acclamation.
passages.later: Deuteronomy said of the king, ‘When he is seated on his royal throne, he must write for himself a copy of this instruction on a scroll’ (Deuteronomy 17:18).
passages.asks: Jehoiada risked everything on a promise God had made about a child. Ask what promise of God you are willing to act on when it looks almost lost. And ask whom you are protecting until their time comes.

passages.t: Treason, a covenant, and a quiet city
passages.happening:
Athaliah hears the noise and comes to the temple. She sees the king standing by his pillar at the entrance, the trumpeters and the people rejoicing, and she tears her clothes and cries treason (verses 12-13). Jehoiada orders her taken out and not killed in the house of the LORD (verse 14). ‘So they seized Athaliah as she reached the entrance of the Horse Gate to the palace grounds, and there they put her to death’ (verse 15).

‘Then Jehoiada made a covenant between himself and the king and the people that they would be the LORD’s people’ (verse 16). The people tear down the temple of Baal and its altars and kill Mattan the priest of Baal (verse 17). Jehoiada restores the temple's order as David had arranged it, sets gatekeepers, and the king is seated on the royal throne (verses 18-20). ‘And all the people of the land rejoiced. And the city was quiet, because Athaliah had been put to the sword’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The chapter moves from secrecy to public celebration, from usurpation to covenant, from Baal to the restored worship of the LORD. The word covenant, berit, comes three times and gives the story its shape: with the commanders, between the assembly and the king, and that king and people would be the LORD's. The scene is full of sound: running, cheering, trumpets, singers, and Athaliah's cry of treason, qesher, against the people restoring the lawful line. The irony is sharp: the usurper accuses the rescuers.

The temple of Baal in Jerusalem was presumably set up under Athaliah, continuing the worship her mother Jezebel had promoted in the north; Jehu had already destroyed Baal's temple in Samaria. Mattan is otherwise unknown. Tearing one's clothes was a sign of grief or alarm. The last verse brings the story to rest: the people rejoiced and the city was quiet.
passages.later: Second Kings tells the same covenant: ‘Then Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people that they would be the LORD’s people’ (2 Kings 11:17).
passages.hard:
Was it right for a priest to lead an armed coup, and to have Athaliah and the priest of Baal killed?

The chapter presents Jehoiada's action as the restoration of the lawful king, not a rebellion. Athaliah had seized the throne by murdering the royal heirs, and in the Chronicler's view she had no right to it; Joash was the heir by God's promise to David. Her death and Mattan's are reported as judgments on murder and on the promotion of Baal worship, which Israel's law treated as capital crimes. Many readers still feel the weight of the violence, and the text tells it briefly.

Christian interpreters have generally treated the chapter as a record of God keeping his promise in Israel's history, not a model for how the church should act. The New Testament gives the church no sword and calls it to suffer rather than seize power. Others have drawn on this chapter in debates about whether it is ever right to resist a tyrant, a question on which Christian traditions have disagreed.
passages.asks: The covenant was that king and people would be the LORD's. Ask what it would mean for you to belong to God first, and to everyone else after. And ask what idol's house in your life needs to come down so that there can be quiet.
